passage_text: Researchers conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of a novel cognitive-behavioral intervention (CBI) on reducing anxiety symptoms among adults with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Eighty participants were randomly assigned to either the CBI group (n=40) or a wait‑list control group (n=40). Baseline assessments revealed comparable anxiety scores across groups (CBI mean 50.2, SD 5.1; control mean 50.4, SD 5.3). Over a 12‑week intervention period, participants in the CBI group received weekly 60‑minute sessions delivered by trained therapists, while controls received no intervention. Post‑intervention anxiety scores were significantly lower in the CBI group (mean 40.5, SD 4.8) compared to controls (mean 52.0, SD 5.3), yielding a p‑value <0.001. A clinically significant response was defined as a drop of at least 5 points from baseline; 30 of 40 CBI participants and 6 of 40 controls met this criterion. The study also measured secondary outcomes, including depressive symptoms and functional impairment, which showed similar patterns of improvement. The authors noted limitations such as a relatively short follow‑up period and the absence of blinding. Despite these constraints, the findings suggest that CBI may be an effective treatment for GAD, warranting further research with larger samples and longer follow‑up.
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of the CBI on anxiety scores as shown in Table 1?
explanation: Correct: B) The CBI group's mean fell from 50.2 to 40.5, and at 12 weeks it was well below the control mean (52.0); the between-group p < 0.001 shows this difference is statistically significant. Why the others are wrong: A) scores fell, not rose. C) the CBI mean dropped by about 10 points. D) baseline, post-treatment and p-values are all reported.
trap: Reading the lower post-treatment number as worse anxiety, when on this scale a lower score means fewer symptoms.

stem: Which experimental design best matches the study described in the passage?
explanation: Participants were randomly assigned to intervention or control groups and followed over time, which is the hallmark of a randomized controlled trial.
trap: Option D (prospective cohort) is often confused with longitudinal designs but lacks randomization.

stem: Calculate the relative risk (RR) of achieving a clinically significant reduction in anxiety for participants in the CBI group compared to the control group. A clinically significant reduction is defined as a 5-point drop from baseline.
explanation: Correct: 30 of 40 CBI participants (75%) and 6 of 40 controls (15%) met the criterion, so RR = 0.75/0.15 = 5.0. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.20 inverts the ratio (control over CBI). B) 0.60 is the absolute risk difference (0.75 - 0.15), not a ratio. D) 17.0 is the odds ratio (30/10 divided by 6/34), not the relative risk.
trap: Reporting the absolute risk difference (0.60) or the odds ratio (17.0) instead of the ratio of the two proportions.

stem: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?

options.A: The follow‑up period was relatively short.
options.C: Secondary outcomes showed improvement patterns similar to the primary outcome.
options.D: Participants who dropped out were excluded from the analysis.

explanation: Correct: The passage never mentions dropouts or exclusions; it reports 40 participants per group and analyzes all of them. Why the others are wrong: A) the authors list a relatively short follow‑up period as a limitation. B) the authors list the absence of blinding as a limitation. C) the passage says secondary outcomes showed similar patterns of improvement.
trap: Assuming dropouts were handled because limitations are listed, when the passage never mentions them.

stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage and Table 1?

options.A: The CBI eliminated anxiety symptoms in every treated participant.
options.B: A greater proportion of CBI participants than control participants had a drop of at least 5 points from baseline.
options.C: The effect of the CBI was shown to persist well beyond the 12‑week period.
options.D: The control group's mean anxiety score fell substantially over the 12 weeks.

explanation: Correct: 30 of 40 CBI participants (75%) versus 6 of 40 controls (15%) met the response criterion. Why the others are wrong: A) only 30 of 40 participants responded and the post‑treatment mean (40.5) is still well above zero. C) the follow‑up period was short, so persistence was not tested. D) the control mean went from 50.4 to 52.0, a slight rise, not a fall.
trap: Treating a significant short-term group difference as proof of universal or lasting benefit.
